With her feet placed on the tips [of his toes], she was repeatedly made to bend low by the weight of her breasts.
Moreover:
"Driven by eagerness, she hastened away with her innate companion, bashfulness;
but led back toward him again by various words from the women of her kinsmen,"
May Gaurī bring you auspiciousness— she who, upon seeing her beloved before her at their first union, was filled with a sense of trepidation,
and whose hair stood on end as she was embraced by the smiling Hara.
Moreover:
By three glances kindled with wrath, these three fires were extinguished; the priests, afflicted by terror, fall down as their turbans are snatched away by the swift-moving hosts below.
Dakṣa offers praise, his wife laments piteously, and even the gods have fled.
May Śiva, who proclaims [his name] with an eternal smile during the ritual of churning the sacrifice for the Goddess, protect you all.
(1.3) Furthermore: Victory to the Lord of the Stars! Homage to the gods!
May the best of the twice-born be free from affliction;
may the earth abound with crops; and may the moon-like king, whose body is as radiant as the moon, shine forth. (1.4)
(1.1) At the end of the *nāndī*, the Stage Manager says:
Enough with this excessive prolixity.

Today, during the spring festival, having been summoned with great honor by the assembly of kings who serve at the lotus feet of His Majesty King Śrī Harṣadeva from various regions and lands, I was addressed as follows:

"We have heard through a succession of reports that our lord, King Śrī Harṣadeva, has composed a short play (*nāṭikā*) named *Ratnāvalī*, adorned with the creation of unprecedented subjects; however, we have not seen it performed.
Therefore, out of respect for that very king—who delights the hearts of all people—and with the intention of showing us favor, you must represent this work in its proper performance."
Therefore, until now, having arranged my costume, I shall accomplish what I desire.
(Walking about and looking around) Ah!
It is my firm conviction that the minds of all the members of the assembly have been captivated. Why?
Because Śrī Harṣa is a skillful poet; this assembly is appreciative of merit; the life of King Vatsarāja is captivating to the world; and we are experts in dramatic performance.
In this world, even a single thing is a means for attaining a desired fruit; how much more so this entire collection of virtues, which has come together through the accumulation of my good fortune!
Therefore, until I go home, summon my wife, and perform a musical concert.
Having walked around and looked toward the tiring-room:
"This is our house; now, I shall enter."
Loudly: Noble lady, please come this way for a moment. (Entering)
Actress:
Noble sir, here I am; may the noble one command me.
"What command is to be carried out?
(1.3) The Stage Manager:
"Noble lady!"
"This assembly of kings is eager to behold the *Ratnāvalī*. Therefore, take up your costume. (1.4) The Actress, with agitation:
Sir,
you are now free from anxiety;
so why do you not dance?
But for me, unfortunate as I am, there is only one daughter;
she too has been given by you to some other land.
With the thought, "How will her marriage take place with a son-in-law residing so far away?", even my own self does not appear before me.
What, then, is to be danced?
(1.5) The Stage Manager:
Noble Lady!
"Enough with this anxiety because he is far away! Look:
when Fate has turned favorable, it brings together one's desired object instantly—whether from another continent, from the middle of the ocean, or even from the ends of the quarters. (1.6)
(1.6) Offstage: Well done, son of Bharata! Well done!
It is even so;
what doubt could there be?
"From another continent," he recites again.
(1.7) The Stage Manager,
having heard this and looking toward the tiring-room, says:
Noble lady,
why do you delay any longer?
Surely this younger brother of mine, who has assumed the role of Yaugandharāyaṇa, has already arrived.
Therefore, come; let us both prepare to enter the dressing room. Thus they both exit.
Thus ends the prologue. Then enters Yaugandharāyaṇa. (1.8) Yaugandharāyaṇa:
It is so;
what doubt could there be?
He recites again: "from another continent."

Otherwise, how could there have been the finding of a plank by the daughter of the King of Siṃhala— who was sought after by a perfected seer and had sunk when her ship was wrecked at sea— and how could there have been the encounter with her in that state by a merchant from Kauśāmbī returning from Siṃhala,
and her being brought here, marked by the jewel-garland?
"In every way, prosperity touches our master," he reflected.
"And by placing her respectfully into the hands of the Queen, I have indeed acted rightly."

And I have heard that even the chamberlain Bābhravya, having with great difficulty crossed the ocean together with Vasubhūti, the minister of the King of Siṃhala, has joined Rumaṇvat, who has gone to destroy Kosala; yet,
even though my purpose is thus nearly accomplished, it does not bring me any peace of mind.
Alas, this state of servitude is indeed miserable! Why so?
Because, at the very outset of this endeavor which is the cause of my master's prosperity, fate has thus provided me with a supporting hand.
"There is no error regarding my success; it is the truth. Nevertheless, acting according to my own will, I am truly afraid of my master. (1.7) A clamor behind the scenes.

Behold, rather, the splendor of the street entrances, resonant with the sounds of drums and the wild clamor of the marketplace on all sides— where the citizens are dancing, seized by their own limbs in the embrace of women intoxicated with honey-wine, while the quarters of the city are being turned tawny by the heaps of scattered flower-powder.
The splendor of the festival of Love. (1.14) The King, looking all around with joy:
Oh!

with floods of *piṣṭātaka* powder that whitened the faces of the day, with *kiṅkirāta* garlands whose tips were bent down by the weight of their golden ornaments and were pale with crushed saffron.

the pavement before one is turned vermilion by the people’s footsteps, which are reddened by the hue of the vermilion falling from the cheeks of unrestrained young women. (1.11)
(1.15) Vidūṣaka: (Looking) Let my dear friend also behold this display of the courtesans, charming with the tinkling sounds of their water-sprinklers filled by very skillful people.
(1.16) King: (Looking)
Friend, you have seen correctly. Why?
Because this place is shrouded in darkness created by scattered fragrant powders.

Beholding this world of serpents, with its slightly visible peaks in the form of upraised hoods and the networks of rays from their jeweled ornaments, it now seems to remind me of the netherworld (pātāla).
(1.17) Vidūṣaka: (looking) Oh friend! Look, look!
"Indeed, here comes Madanikā herself, dancing a spring dance worthy of Love, together with Cūtalatā.

The southern breeze blows, acting as a dear messenger for the flower-armed god of love; it possesses many blossoms as its crest-jewels and has loosened its grasp.
The assembly of young women, their sorrow increased by separation, longing for union with their beloveds, and unable to endure the waiting, languishes.
Here, first the month of Madhu makes the hearts of people soft;
afterwards, Kāma pierces them with flower-arrows that have found their opportunity. 15.

Their disheveled mass of hair, having become loose, abandons the beauty of the arranged floral wreath.
As she plays, these two anklets of the intoxicated woman, clinging to her feet, cry out all the more;
and this necklace, displaced by the continuous trembling, incessantly strikes her chest, as if out of pity for her waist— which bends under the weight of her breasts— disregarding its own fracture.
(1.20) Vidūṣaka: Oh, friend!

I have danced.
(1.31) King: Well done! (1.32) Cūtalatikā: Friend Madanikā!

let us first report the message of the Great King to the Queen.
(1.33) Madanikā: Come!
Let us hasten.
(She walks about and approaches.)
(1.34) Both: "Victory! Victory to the Lord!
"The Queen commands...

"No, no! Inform [the King]!

"Indeed, the mere command 'So be it' is most delightful, especially today on this great festival of Love.
Therefore, let it be said:
what does the Goddess command?"

Today, having gone to the Māraṇdu garden, I must perform a worship of the divine Flower-Arrowed One (Kusumāyudha) stationed at the red *aśoka* tree.
My noble lord should be present there. (1.38) King: Friend!
What is to be said?
One festival has led directly into another.
(1.39) Vidūṣaka: So, rise up!
"Let us go right there, so that even for me, a brahmin who has gone there, there may be some auspicious blessing.
(1.40) King: Madanikā, go and inform the Queen.
"I have indeed arrived at the Makaranda garden.
(1.41) The two maidservants: "As the master commands. [They exit.]
(1.42) King: Friend, come, let us descend.

(1.43) King: Friend, show me the way to the Makaranda garden.
(1.44) Vidūṣaka: This way, this way, your honor.
Thus they walk about.
(1.45) Vidūṣaka: (looking ahead) Oh!
"This is the Makaranda garden;
come, let us enter. Thus they both enter.
(1.46) Vidūṣaka: [With astonishment] Oh, Great King!
Look, look!

This is that Makaranda Garden, appearing as if it were a messenger sent to announce your arrival; it is delightful with the sweet songs of intoxicated cuckoos mingled with the humming of swarms of bees, while the dust from the clusters of Sahakāra blossoms— shaken by the Malaya breeze— is caught in the webs of spiderwebs.
Therefore, let my dear friend look around.
(1.47) King: (Looking all around) Oh, what delightful beauty this Makaranda garden possesses! For here indeed—
Bearing a coppery luster with sprouts possessing the glow of rising coral,
assuming the playful sport of indistinct chatter through the sweet warbling of swarms of bees,
they sway repeatedly with clusters of branches trembling in the Malaya breeze.
Having now encountered the intoxication of honey, these trees appear as if they have become drunk.

Furthermore: At their roots, the *bakula* trees vomit forth a rain of flowers like a mouthful of wine; and upon the young woman’s moon-like face, copper-red with honey, the *campaka* blossoms finally shine today after a long time.

And having heard the intense tinkling of anklets upon the trampling of the feet of the Aśoka tree, the swarms of bees begin as if to imitate it with their humming songs. (1.18) Vidūṣaka: (Having heard it)
O friend,
these bees do not imitate the sound of anklets;
this is surely the sound of the anklets belonging to the Queen’s attendants.
(1.49) King: Friend, you have understood correctly.
Then enter Vāsavadattā, Kāñcanamālā, Sāgarikā, and the retinue according to their rank.

(1.51) Kāñcanamālā: Come, come, mistress!
(1.52) Vāsavadattā: [Enter.]
(Walking about) Maid Kañcanamālā!
Now, how far away is that red *aśoka* tree where I must perform the worship of the blessed God of Love?
(1.53) Kāñcanamālā:
My lady,
it is indeed very near.
Does the lady not see?
This is indeed the Mādhavī creeper, possessed by the lady, which is beautiful with flowers blooming incessantly.
And this is another, a *nomālikā* creeper, for which the lord, longing for the emergence of its first blossoms, has directed his own gaze.
Therefore, having passed this, that very red *aśoka* tree is visible, where the Queen will perform her worship.
(1.54) Vāsavadattā: Therefore, come.
"Let us go there. (1.55) Kāñcanamālā: "Come, come, my lady!"
All walk around. Vāsavadattā:
Ah, this is that red *aśoka* tree where I shall perform the worship.
"In that case, bring me the offerings for my worship.
(1.57) Sāgarikā approaches and says:
"My lady!"
"All this is ready. (1.58) Vāsavadattā, having observed, [says] to herself:
Oh, the negligence of the attendants!
She would have fallen right within the range of vision of the very person whose path of sight she is guarding.
Very well, let it be so for now.
(Aloud) Girl Sārikā! Why have you come here today, leaving Sārikā behind, while the attendants are occupied with the festival of Love?
Therefore, go there quickly;
deliver all these offerings for the worship into the hands of Kāñcanamālā. Sāgarikā: As the Queen commands.
Having done so and walked a few steps, she said to herself:
"I have entrusted Sārikā into the hands of Susaṅgatā;
nevertheless, I still feel a curiosity to see her."
Is it just as the blessed god of love is worshipped in the inner apartments of His Majesty, or is it exactly the same here? Or could it be otherwise?
Therefore, I shall observe this while remaining unobserved.
(Walking about and looking around.)
"Until it is time for the worship here, I too shall gather flowers to worship the blessed Madana himself.
Thus she mimes the gathering of flowers.
(1.60) Vāsavadattā.
Kāñcanamālā: "Kāñcanamāle, escort the venerable Pajjunna! (1.61) Kāñcanamālā: [She does so.]
"As the mistress commands. [She] does so.
(1.62) Vidūṣaka: [Walking about and looking around.]
O friend,
since the sound of the anklets is so tranquil, I suspect that the Queen has arrived at the foot of the Ashoka tree.
(1.63) King: Friend, you have understood correctly. Behold:
she, whose form is as delicate as a flower, maintains her waist with such extreme slenderness through her religious observances.
She shines like the staff of the bow standing at the side of the god whose banner is the sea-monster.
Therefore come; let us approach. Having approached, O dear Vāsavadattā!
(1.64) Vāsavadattā / Having looked / How is this?
Noble sir! Victory, victory to the noble sir!
May you grace this place by accepting a seat.
"Here is a seat; let my noble lord sit here. The King sits down with a dramatic gesture.
(1.65) Kāñcanamālā: Mistress,
let the venerable Pajjunna be worshipped after the red *aśoka* tree has been made beautiful with handfuls of flowers, saffron, and sandalwood offered by her own hand.
(1.66) Vāsavadattā: Therefore, bring me the materials for the preliminary worship.
(1.67) Kāñcanamālā brings them forward.
(1.68) Vāsavadattā does so. (1.69) The King: My dear Vāsavadattā, your beauty is rendered exceptionally radiant by your recent bath.
With the lovely ends of your shimmering silken garment radiant with safflower dye,
you shine like a creeper sprouting from a branch of young coral, honoring the god whose banner is the sea-monster. (1.20)
Moreover: "O beloved, this *aśoka* tree, touched by your hand while it was occupied with the worship of the God of Love, appears as if its other, most tender sprouts have burst forth.
(1.21) Furthermore: "Today, this bodiless one (*anaṅga*) will surely condemn his own bodilessness."
"That he has not yet attained the festival of the touch of your hand. (1.22) (1.70) Kāñcanamālā:
"My lady!"
"Welcome, noble Pajjunna! Therefore, please pay your respects and honor to my lord.
Vāsavadattā.
"In that case, then bring me flowers and ointment.
Kāñcanamālā:
"My lady!"
"All this is prepared.

(1.74) Sāgarikā has taken up flowers.
Alas, alas!
How is it that I have waited so long, my heart pierced by the thorn of love?
Therefore, having become a cloud by means of this cluster of *sinduvāra* flowers, I shall look.
(Looking) What?
"The Lord Flower-Arrowed One himself is receiving worship right here before my eyes;
therefore, standing right here with these flowers, I too shall worship the Lord Flower-Arrowed One.
(She says this and casts down the flowers.)
Homage to you, O Blessed One, Flower-Armed!
You shall be one whose vision is unfailing for me.
That which was to be seen has been seen.
Thus he bows.
It is wonderful!
Though seen, he must be seen again.
"I shall depart while no one yet sees me.

Today, Vasantaka!
Come;
now you shall receive your reward for ensuring our safety.

"Today, Vasantaka!

When the sun, whose light has cast away all darkness, has reached the farthest limit of the sky,
and the assembly of kings has gathered together at the time of the evening court,
they come now indeed to serve your feet, which possess the luster of the morning lotus.
Produced by the excellence of her joy, it is gazed upon like the rising of the moon by the eyes of Udayana. // 23 //

This body of mine, which has been made to perform the service of another, has become highly honored by the sight of him.
King: How so? Even the passing of the twilight was not noticed by us, whose minds were captivated by the festival. Queen: Look, my lord!
This eastern quarter, with the sun partially hidden behind the edge of the mountain, indicates the presence of the Lord of Night.
With her face turned very pale, the beautiful woman seemed to hold something unpleasant within her heart.
"O Goddess, therefore arise;
let us enter within the dwelling.
Having all arisen, they walk around.
(1.82) Sāgarikā: How so?
The Queen has departed.
Very well.
"I shall go quickly.
Having seen the king full of longing and having sighed, [he said]:
"Alas, alas!"
"By me, of such feeble fortune, this person was not even permitted to be gazed upon for long.

O Queen, behold how the lotuses suddenly lose their luster, surpassed by the splendor of your lotus-face which eclipses the moon;
and hearing the songs of your retinue of courtesans, the female bees [desert the flowers].

that you still long to see him again, by the mere sight of whom such torment was felt—oh, what delusion is yours! O heart, you are most ungrateful.

O Lord Kusumāyudha!
